title: Boss: the Dockerfile reviewer
summary: Three image tickets on a real Docker Engine: read an image you did not build, repair a multi-stage build, make a slow build fast.

steps.title: The review bot
body: Image tickets reach you from every direction: a vendor image nobody can explain, a Dockerfile a teammate "tidied up",
a CI job that rebuilds everything on every commit. Each ticket below opens its own machine with a **real Docker
Engine** and the problem already on it. Use `docker image inspect -f`, `docker history --no-trunc`, `docker build`

steps.title: Ticket 1: "what does this vendor image do?"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. Security asks about `vendor/reporting:3.2`, an image with no Dockerfile in
sight. Read it **without running it**, and answer:
1. `~/answers/port.txt`: the port it says it listens on;
3. `~/answers/command.txt`: the full command a plain `docker run vendor/reporting:3.2` starts (entrypoint, then
4. `~/answers/leak.txt`: the password that one of its build steps wrote and then deleted. (Deleting a file in a
later step does not remove it from the image.)

checks.name: port.txt is the exposed port
checks.fail: Not the exposed port. `docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.ExposedPorts}}' vendor/reporting:3.2`.

checks.name: user.txt is the user it runs as
checks.fail: Not the image's user. `docker image inspect -f '{{.Config.User}}' ...`.

checks.name: command.txt is entrypoint plus default arguments
checks.fail: Not the full command. It is the Entrypoint's items followed by the Cmd's: `docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}} {{json .Config.Cmd}}'`.

checks.name: leak.txt has the leaked password
checks.fail: Not the leaked password. `docker history --no-trunc vendor/reporting:3.2` prints every build step's full command.

hints: `docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config}}' vendor/reporting:3.2 | jq` shows the user, ports, entrypoint and cmd.
`docker history --no-trunc --format '{{.CreatedBy}}' vendor/reporting:3.2` lists the commands that built each layer.
The password is in a `RUN` line that writes `/root/.netrc`.
steps.explain: An image documents itself: its config holds the user, ports, environment and start command, and its history holds every build command, secrets included. That is why a credential written in one `RUN` and deleted in the next is still leaked (`docker save` would even extract the file), and why build secrets go in `RUN --mount=type=secret` instead.

steps.title: Ticket 2: "the multi-stage build broke"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. A teammate tidied up `~/tool/Dockerfile` and now
`docker build -t shop/tool:1.0 ~/tool` fails. Read the error, fix the Dockerfile (keep its three stages: assemble,
check, small final image), and build `shop/tool:1.0` so that `docker run --rm shop/tool:1.0` prints `tool 1.0 ok`.
The final image must stay on `busybox:1.37`, with only the tool in `/opt/tool`.

checks.name: docker build succeeds
checks.fail: `docker build -t shop/tool:1.0 ~/tool` still fails. Read the first error line: which stage name does it not know?

checks.name: docker run prints tool 1.0 ok
checks.fail: The image does not print `tool 1.0 ok`.

checks.name: the final image is busybox with only the tool
checks.cmd: docker run --rm --entrypoint sh shop/tool:1.0 -c 'test ! -e /etc/alpine-release && test ! -e /src && ls /opt/tool' | sort | xargs
checks.fail: The final image should be `busybox:1.37` with only `tool.sh` and `VERSION` in `/opt/tool`.

checks.name: there are still three stages
checks.fail: Keep the three stages (assemble, check, final): rename, do not delete.

hints: `docker build` names the problem: a stage that copies from a name no stage has, and two stages with one name.
Stage names must be unique; `COPY --from=NAME` must name an earlier stage (or an image).
Name the second stage `check` (`FROM build AS check`), and copy from `build`: `COPY --from=build /out/ /opt/tool/`.
solution: sed -i 's/^FROM build AS build$/FROM build AS check/; s/--from=builder/--from=build/' ~/tool/Dockerfile
steps.explain: Stage names are how stages refer to each other, so they must be unique and spelled the same in `COPY --from`. Note what BuildKit did with the `check` stage: the final stage does not depend on it, so a plain `docker build` skips it entirely. To run such a test stage in CI, build it on purpose: `docker build --target check .`.

steps.title: Ticket 3: "CI rebuilds everything on every commit"
prompt: A real Docker Engine runs in this terminal. Every commit to `~/web` reinstalls its packages, and the build sends a
20 MB `logs/` folder and the `.git` folder to the builder each time. Fix `~/web` so that:
1. changing anything under `logs/` (or `.git/`) does **not rebuild the image at all**;
2. changing `src/server.sh` reuses the cached install, while changing `packages.txt` reinstalls;
4. `docker run --rm shop/web:dev` (build it with that name) prints `web up with 2 packages`.

checks.name: the image builds and runs
checks.cmd: cd ~/web && docker build -q -t shop/web:dev . >/dev/null && docker run --rm shop/web:dev
checks.fail: `docker build` fails, or the app does not print `web up with 2 packages`.

checks.name: logs/ and .git are not in the image
logs/ changes do not rebuild; src changes keep the install; packages.txt changes reinstall
checks.fail: The check builds a copy of `~/web` and changes `logs/today.log`, `src/server.sh`, then `packages.txt`. Use a `.dockerignore`, and copy only what the install needs before running it.

hints: Two separate problems: what is sent to the builder (`.dockerignore`), and the instruction order (cache).
`.dockerignore` with `logs/` and `.git` keeps them out of the context, so they can neither bust the cache nor end up in a layer.
solution: docker build --progress=plain -t shop/web:dev . 2>&1 | grep -E 'transferring context|CACHED|DONE' | tail -n 6
steps.explain: `.dockerignore` decides what the builder can see: ignored files are never sent (the context shrank from 20 MB to a few KB), so they can neither invalidate a cached `COPY . .` nor leak into a layer. Ordering decides what each change costs. Together they turn "every commit reinstalls" into "only a dependency change reinstalls", and on CI that is the difference between seconds and minutes per build.
